NASA SPLASH · OSDR hardware registry · OpenFOAM v2606

Which spaceflight biology hardware can be modelled?

A metadata audit of NASA's space-biology hardware catalogues, a minimum-information checklist for computational fluid dynamics (CFD) of specimen environments, and verified three-dimensional transient OpenFOAM models, in flight (0 g) and ground control (1 g), of the hardware whose parameters can be sourced.

Richard Barker · source snapshot 2026-10-12 · {{hwNEntities}} hardware entities · {{hwNHabitats}} specimen habitats · {{hwNCuratedA}} hardware items modelled

Read the manuscript PDF Supplement (PDF) Word (.docx) Code & data (GitHub)

Overview

The specimen environment inside flight hardware is rarely documented well enough to model.

Spaceflight biology results are interpreted against the hardware the specimens lived in, yet the physical environment inside that hardware (airflow, gas composition, temperature, humidity, light and nutrient delivery) is rarely documented well enough to be modelled. We joined the three public NASA hardware sources (the SPLASH instrument catalogue, the OSDR hardware registry and the experiment-platform field of every OSDR study), scored every specimen-housing item against a 15-item checklist of what a CFD model needs, curated the literature for the most-used hardware, and built verified OpenFOAM models of the hardware that reached CFD readiness.

01Where the hardware flies and how specimens are fed

From all catalogued hardware to the items whose public metadata support a CFD model.

The crosswalk produced {{hwNEntities}} entities. {{hwNBioCapable}} can carry space-biology payloads and {{hwNHabitats}} house live specimens during flight; only {{hwNHabUsed}} of these are linked to at least one OSDR study. Mission records place bio-capable hardware on the Space Shuttle ({{hwNPlatShuttle}}), on free-flying biosatellites ({{hwNPlatFreeFlyerBionCosmosBiosatellite}}) and on the ISS ({{hwNPlatIss}}). Nutrient delivery was evidenced for fewer than half of the habitats ({{hwNNutNoneEvidenced}} with no evidence); where evidenced, animal food and water ({{hwNNutAnimalFoodWater}}), culture medium ({{hwNNutLiquidCultureMedium}}) and agar ({{hwNNutAgarGel}}) were the commonest modes. Every assigned mode is backed by a verbatim quotation.

02Catalogue defects

Errors that propagate silently into any automated reuse of the catalogues.

{{hwNSplashBlock}} SPLASH records (#121–#147) carry descriptive fields displaced from neighbouring rows: {{hwNSplashMisattributed}} fields were confirmed as misattributed on review. For example, a Plant Growth Unit record's specimen field describes an RNA thermal cycler, and a BRIC-Opti canister record carries the crop list and the CO₂, humidity and temperature control ranges of the Advanced Plant Habitat. The sources, schematics and study_links fields are empty in every record. {{hwNDatasetsNoPlatform}} of {{hwNDatasets}} OSDR datasets have no experiment-platform entry; the rest use {{hwNPlatformStrings}} free-text strings, with {{hwNVeggieSpellings}} spellings of Veggie alone.

The displaced block is excluded from every analysis here (data/curated/splash_block_rule.yaml, with a reviewed verdict for each flagged field in data/curated/splash_field_review.csv). Anyone reusing SPLASH records #121–#147 should check name, background and descriptive fields against each other first.

03The MI-CFD-HW checklist

Fifteen items a CFD model of a specimen environment needs; six are critical.

An item is Tier A (CFD-ready) when every critical item is sourced; the airflow requirement is waived for sealed or passive hardware. Specimen type is almost always stated ({{hwItemBOneQuant}}% quantitative), but airflow rate ({{hwItemFTwoQuant}}%), specimen metabolic load ({{hwItemBThreeQuant}}%) and heat load ({{hwItemTOneQuant}}%) are almost never given. Median completeness was {{hwComplMedianPublic}} using all public sources and {{hwComplMedianSplash}} using SPLASH alone.

04Which hardware is under-documented

Documentation tracks use, platform and hardware class, not era.

Completeness differed by hardware class (Kruskal–Wallis p = {{hwKWHwClassP}}), flight platform (p = {{hwKWPlatformP}}) and catalogue coverage (p = {{hwKWCoverageP}}), but not by era (p = {{hwKWEraP}}) or SPLASH status (p = {{hwKWStatusP}}). Cell and microbe culture hardware was least documented and ISS hardware best. Hardware used in OSDR studies was better documented than unused hardware (p = {{hwKWUsedP}}; Spearman ρ = {{hwRhoUse}} with the number of studies), but several used items remain below the median, and some of the most-used hardware cannot be modelled: the ISS Rodent Habitat, linked to {{hwNStudiesRodentHabitat}} OSDR studies, has no published internal cage dimensions in any source we could open, and BRIC-PDFU, linked to {{hwNStudiesBricPdfu}} studies, has no published internal dimensions.

05Validating the scorer

Two blind raters, an adjudicated gold standard, and a conservative automated scorer.

Two raters scored a random sample of 12 habitats blind; they agreed on {{hwValRaterExact}}% of 180 cells (weighted κ = {{hwValRaterKappa}}). Against the adjudicated gold standard the automated scorer never credited absent information (precision {{hwValPrecision}}) but missed some (recall {{hwValRecall}}; mean completeness {{hwValAutoMean}} versus {{hwValGoldMean}} gold), so automated completeness is a conservative lower bound. No sampled entity was Tier A on the gold scores either.

07Literature curation

Papers, technical reports and mission documentation, one verbatim quotation per value.

Curation of {{hwNCurated}} hardware items yielded {{hwNCuratedSourced}} sourced parameters out of {{hwNCuratedParams}} sought ({{hwPctCuratedSourced}}%). {{hwNCuratedA}} items reached Tier A (the Advanced Plant Habitat, the JAXA Aquatic Habitat, the Mice Drawer System and the Vented Fly Box), {{hwNCuratedB}} remained Tier B and {{hwNCuratedC}} Tier C. The commonest gap is the airflow that ventilates the specimens, missing for {{hwNMissingFTwo}} curated items. An independent audit found all {{hwNAuditQuoteFound}} of {{hwNAudit}} sampled quotations in their sources.

08Solver verification

OpenFOAM v2606 (buoyantBoussinesqPimpleFoam) against benchmark and analytic solutions.

The solver reproduced the reference heated-cavity Nusselt numbers with second-order convergence (observed order {{hwVerPRaFive}} and {{hwVerPRaSix}} at Ra = 105 and 106); Richardson-extrapolated values were within {{hwVerMaxExtErr}}% of Hortmann et al. (1990). One-dimensional diffusion matched the analytic solution to {{hwVerDiffMaxErr}} (concentration scale 0–1), and the transient CO₂ balance closed to within {{hwCfdMaxImbalance}}% in every hardware run. Grid convergence indices were computed for {{hwNGciQuantities}} quantities on three-mesh ladders ({{hwNGciMonotonic}} converging monotonically; median fine-mesh GCI {{hwGciMedian}}%, maximum {{hwGciMax}}%; full table in the supplement).

09Specimen environments, flight versus ground

Three-dimensional transient models of the four CFD-ready items, at 0 g and 1 g.

  • Mice Drawer System. With the sourced cage through-flow and organism-level loads for a 30 g mouse, the air around the mouse carried {{hwCfdMdsZeroCo}} ppm more CO₂ than the supply, was {{hwCfdMdsZeroDt}} K warmer and had a mean age of {{hwCfdMdsZeroAge}} s. Flight and ground control differed by {{hwCfdMdsGravityDiffPct}}%: the forced flow dominates the mouse's buoyant plume (Ri = {{hwCfdMdsZeroRi}}).
  • Advanced Plant Habitat. At the PH-04 set-points the canopy CO₂ excess was {{hwCfdAphZeroCo}} ppm relative to the supply in flight (s.d. {{hwCfdAphZeroCoSd}}) and {{hwCfdAphOneCo}} ppm in ground control (s.d. {{hwCfdAphOneCoSd}}), a difference within the fluctuation of the transitional, fan-driven flow. At maximum fan speed it was {{hwCfdAphFanmaxZeroCo}} ppm.
  • Vented Fly Box. The box exchanges gas with the cabin only through its vents, whose size is not published. With 20 mm vents the CO₂ excess at the vial plugs reached {{hwCfdVfbSmallZeroCo}} ppm, with 60 mm vents {{hwCfdVfbLargeZeroCo}} ppm: {{hwCfdVfbCoRatio}}-fold from one undocumented parameter.
  • Aquatic Habitat. At the sourced flow per aquarium, the mean age of water was {{hwCfdAqhZeroAge}} s against a nominal residence time of {{hwCfdAqhZeroTau}} s, which indicates poorly flushed regions for the assumed port positions.

10What the models can and cannot say

Undocumented inputs can matter more than gravity.

In the four hardware items that could be modelled, the gravity contrast was small: forced ventilation dominated the mouse-cage environment, and in the plant growth chamber the flight–ground difference was within the fluctuation of the flow. This is not evidence that gravity does not matter to these environments, because the loads that would let it act (canopy and lamp heat, fly metabolic heat, the solutal buoyancy of exhaled CO₂) are exactly the inputs the public record does not provide. For hardware of this kind, interpreting a flight–ground difference as a gravity effect requires the hardware environment to be measured or modelled, and modelling requires metadata that do not yet exist publicly.

Recommendations for SPLASH and the OSDR registry

  1. Adopt the MI-CFD-HW items as structured fields with units and provenance.
  2. Populate the existing but empty sources, schematics and study_links fields.
  3. Replace the free-text experiment-platform field of OSDR studies with a controlled reference to a hardware identifier.
  4. Record, per flight, the logged temperature, humidity and CO₂ of the hardware interior.
Limitations: the automated scorer is conservative, so its tiers are a lower bound. Curation was bounded by access to sources. The CFD models are laminar and Boussinesq in temperature only: solutal buoyancy is reported as a Rayleigh number, not simulated. Heat loads that could not be sourced were not invented, so the gravity contrasts are lower bounds. Unpublished details are declared assumptions and, where they matter, were varied.
